rv.q: What makes 'The Country House' worth seeing is that Mr. Harmon has written a play in which all of his characters, even the least sympathetic ones, are recognizably human.
Come to think of it, this comfort-food of a play by Donald Margulies (“Time Stands Still”) is like Goldilocks’ porridge: not too hot, not too cold — just . . . lukewarm.
Too often, though, it brings to mind another throwback: the formulaic star vehicle that relied upon its leading lady’s allure to disguise its flimsiness.
Unfortunately, the same might be said — with a bit of a twist — to these characters: You’re interesting, but not interesting enough.
While it may be churlish to complain about a play that amuses and entertains with such efficiency, The Country House is disappointingly toothless, even bland.

Mostly what emerges is a lumpy, sour mess.
Except for the fine cast led by the formidably elegant Blythe Danner, however, there is little else that feels right enough about "The Country House."
As a result, The Country House is an entertaining evening of theater, even if it isn't a particularly enlightening one.
Narcissism and banality are, after all, hardly unique to one character in The Country House.
And aside from one exceptional performance, this clichéd, but ultimately harmless, comedy-drama directed by Daniel Sullivan is an old-fashioned, by-the-numbers affair.
This is a harmless piece of fluff that is beautifully executed but won’t stick to your ribs.

cn.t: Critics find this Chekhov-inspired family drama pleasant but predictable, with Blythe Danner's luminous performance elevating familiar material. Most agree it pales beside Durang's sharper "Vanya and Sonia," offering polished but unremarkable theatre.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.
